judgments.catchwords: Enclosure 186 was the Defendant’s application which sought the Court to decide first whether the Plaintiff was present at the Defendant's residence on the day in question. The Defendant further sought to do this on affidavits, in camera or via remote communication technology. The Plaintiff, meanwhile, argued that this was a delaying tactic and that the disputed, credibility-driven facts surely needed a full trial. The Court allowed the application in part. To this end, the Court held that Order 33 rule 2 of the Rules of Court 2012 also covered the disputed facts. Presence must logically precede any sexual assault, so deciding on it first would definitely save time and costs, whichever way it goes. However, the Court refused to determine this by way of affidavit evidence. Instead, the Court ordered a trial of the preliminary issues on oral evidence with cross-examination, held via Zoom and open to the public and press. All other proceedings were stayed, and costs were made costs in the cause.

judgments.catchwords: Offence under section 39B(1)(a) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 read together with section 34 of the Penal Code - Whether the trial judge should have informed at the close of the prosecution's case, that the defence was being called upon to answer a case of actual trafficking or presumed trafficking? - Overwhelming evidence proved the elements of custody, control, and knowledge - Actual possession of the impugned drugs was established - Section 180 (1) and (4) of the Criminal Procedure Code - Procedure after conclusion of case for prosecution - No statutory or legal requirement to state the presumption when calling for the defence - Formal verbal label for an evidentiary rule at the close of the prosecution's case is unnecessary - Statutory presumption of trafficking under section 37(da)(xvi) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 - Section 422 of the Criminal Procedure Code - Not vitiate the conviction - No miscarriage of justice - Failure either to make or to record such a finding does not ipso facto - The law does not require a mini-judgment or detailed legal reasons at the close of the prosecution’s case

FAMILY LAW Adultery — Proof — Circumstantial evidence — Standard of proof on balance of probabilities — Proof of inclination and opportunity — Husband and co-respondent sharing registered JPN residential address, joint overseas border crossings, Facebook two-year anniversary post, and sham automotive workshop setup — Evidence Act 1950, s. 101 — Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976, s. 54(1)(a). FAMILY LAW Matrimonial assets — Division — Matrimonial home sold unilaterally by husband — Gross sale price of RM680,000.00 — Husband asserting net balance after bank loan redemption but failing to produce redemption statement — Full and frank financial disclosure — Duty of parties — Duty of utmost good faith — Adverse inference drawn against husband — Evidence Act 1950, s. 114(g) — Divisible pool assessed at gross sale price of RM680,000.00 — Equal 50% division awarded to wife (RM340,000.00) — Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976, s. 76. judgments.title: BELLWORTH DEVELOPMENTS SDN BHD v SETIAKON BUILDERS SDN BHD
judgments.catchwords: The Court of Appeal reaffirmed the principle of minimal judicial intervention in arbitration. A procedural breach, such as an alleged one-day delay in submitting a draft award for AIAC technical review, does not automatically invalidate an arbitral award where the requirement is merely directory, no timely objection was raised, and no prejudice is shown. An arbitral award will not be set aside on the basis of a purported “new difference” where the issue was within the parties’ pleadings, evidence and submissions. Courts will not review the merits of an award under the guise of a setting-aside application.’

judgments.title: BELLWORTH DEVELOPMENTS SDN BHD v SETIAKON BUILDERS SDN BHD
judgments.catchwords: The Court of Appeal reaffirmed the principle of minimal judicial intervention in arbitration. A procedural breach, such as an alleged one-day delay in submitting a draft award for AIAC technical review, does not automatically invalidate an arbitral award where the requirement is merely directory, no timely objection was raised, and no prejudice is shown. An arbitral award will not be set aside on the basis of a purported “new difference” where the issue was within the parties’ pleadings, evidence and submissions. Courts will not review the merits of an award under the guise of a setting-aside application.
